explanation: The center consists of moves commuting with everything. The centralizer of a subgroup fixes it pointwise by conjugation, while the normalizer fixes it setwise. The normalizer is the largest subgroup of $G$ in which $H$ is normal.

pitfall: The target is the image, not automatically all of the codomain. A non-surjective map does not yield $G/\ker$ $\varphi \cong H$.
prompt: Map $C_{6}$ to $C_{3}$ and inspect the two-element fibers before collapsing them.
proof: Equality of kernel cosets is equivalent to $\varphi (g)=\varphi (h)$, proving both well-definedness and injectivity of the factor map. Its multiplication law follows from $\varphi$, and surjectivity follows from restricting the target to $\operatorname{im}\varphi$.

paragraphs: The map $H\to HN/N$ has kernel $H\cap N$. Hence $H/(H\cap N)\cong HN/N$. Quotienting in stages similarly gives $(G/K)/(H/K)\cong G/H$ for $K\le H$ normal in $G$. Subgroups above a kernel correspond exactly to subgroups of the image.

definition: N\le H\le G,\quad N,H\trianglelefteq G,\qquad (G/N)/(H/N)\cong G/H

intuition: Forgetting $N$ and then forgetting the rest of $H$ has the same effect as forgetting $H$ at once.
pitfall: Normality of $N$ in $H$ and $H$ in $G$ alone does not imply normality of $N$ in $G$. Check both required quotient groups exist.
prompt: Follow both routes from $G$ to $G/M$: quotient directly by $M$, or first by $N$ and then by $M/N$. Why does every element reach the same final coset?

explanation: The same group can act on many sets, and even on the same set in different ways. Polygon symmetries act on vertices, edges and diagonals. The group also acts on itself by left multiplication or by conjugation, which are different actions.

reading.title: Every orbit is a coset action
paragraphs: An action is a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Sym}(X)$. The left regular action is faithful, proving Cayley. Each action splits uniquely into orbits, and $gG_x\mapsto gx$ identifies an orbit with $G/G_x$. Stabilizers along an orbit are conjugate.

An equivariant map can only enlarge a point stabilizer. More explicitly, a map $G/H\to G/K$ taking $H$ to $aK$ exists exactly when $H\le aKa^{-1}$. The two transitive actions are isomorphic exactly when their stabilizers are conjugate.

explanation: The orbit is a subset of the acted-on set. The stabilizer is a subgroup of $G$. Points in one orbit have conjugate stabilizers. A transitive action has a single orbit and is equivalent as a $G$-set to the action on cosets of one stabilizer.
intuition: A point's orbit records where it can go; its stabilizer records moves that leave it where it is.
pitfall: The bijection is an isomorphism of $G$-sets, not generally of groups: neither the orbit nor the coset set need have a group structure.
prompt: Pick a square vertex and then an edge. Count the orbit and stabilizer each time.
proof: The map $gG_x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is well-defined because stabilizer elements fix $x$. It is onto by the definition of orbit, and $g\cdot x=h\cdot x$ exactly when $h^{-1}g$ belongs to $G_x$. Thus it is bijective, giving the count.

explanation: The stabilizer under conjugation is the centralizer. Central elements form singleton classes. In $S_n$, two permutations are conjugate exactly when their disjoint cycle types agree. This classification foreshadows characters, which are constant on conjugacy classes.
intuition: Conjugation changes labels while preserving the intrinsic type of a move. Its orbits are conjugacy classes.
pitfall: Having the same order is weaker than having the same conjugacy class. Equal cycle type characterizes conjugacy in $S_n$, not automatically in $A_n$.
prompt: Partition $S_{3}$ into its identity, transpositions and 3-cycles, and verify $6=1+3+2$.

intuition: A subgroup with few cosets makes the whole group permute a small set. The kernel is what every coset fails to detect.

explanation: Double cosets partition $G$, but they need not have equal sizes. Their sizes depend on the overlap between $H$ and $gKg^{-1}$. View them through the action of $H$ on the coset set $G/K$.

explanation: Both $G$ and $X$ are finite. The group need not act faithfully. A fixed configuration may have many moved positions: only the assigned data must agree after the move. Stabilizers account for the unequal sizes of orbits.

explanation: The largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$ is the order of a Sylow $p$-subgroup. More strongly, $G$ contains a subgroup of order $p^j$ for every $0\le j\le a$. The case $j=1$ produces an element of order $p$, which is Cauchy's theorem.
intuition: Prime-power divisors are special: unlike arbitrary divisors, they always occur as subgroup orders.
pitfall: Lagrange's converse is false for general divisors; Sylow supplies the prime-power cases. A Sylow $p$-subgroup is maximal among $p$-subgroups, not necessarily among all proper subgroups.

explanation: More generally, every $p$-subgroup is contained in a conjugate of any chosen Sylow $p$-subgroup. Thus a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal, and a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup is unique. Conjugating subgroups is an action whose stabilizer is a normalizer.
intuition: A finite group can have several Sylow $p$-subgroups, but all have the same internal shape because conjugation moves any one to another.
pitfall: Arbitrary subgroups of the same order need not be conjugate. The maximal $p$-power hypothesis is essential.
prompt: Follow the three Sylow 2-subgroups of $D_{6}$ under conjugation.
proof: Let a $p$-subgroup $H$ act on $G/Q$, where $Q$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup. The index of $Q$ is coprime to $p$, and orbit sizes are powers of $p$, so some coset $gQ$ is fixed. Thus $H\subseteq gQg^{-1}$. If $H$ is also Sylow, equal orders make this inclusion an equality.

explanation: These are necessary restrictions, not a promise that every allowed number occurs. Combining the restrictions for different primes with element counting can rule out simplicity. paragraphs: If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $P$ is Sylow in $G$, then $P\cap N$ is Sylow in $N$ and $PN/N$ is Sylow in $G/N$. Compute orders using $|PN|=|P||N|/|P\cap N|$ and compare their prime parts.

For primes $p>q$, a group of order $pq$ has a normal subgroup of order $p$. It is cyclic unless $q$ divides $p-1$; in that case exactly one additional nonabelian isomorphism type arises from a nontrivial action $C_q\to\operatorname{Aut}(C_p)$.

definition: G\text{ simple}\iff G\ne\{e\}\ \text{and}\ \{e\},G\text{ are its only normal subgroups}
explanation: A composition series is a finite chain in which each subgroup is normal in the preceding one and each successive quotient is simple. The Jordan–$H$ölder theorem says that any two such series have the same simple factors up to isomorphism and reordering. The source mentions this theorem without proving it.
intuition: Normal subgroups allow a group to be broken into quotient pieces. Simple groups are the nontrivial pieces that cannot be broken further in this way.
pitfall: A composition series requires normality in the preceding subgroup, not necessarily in all of $G$. Composition factors do not by themselves determine the original group.

reading.title: Composition factors versus chief factors
paragraphs: A composition series has simple successive factors and only requires each term to be normal in the preceding term. A chief series requires all terms to be normal in the whole group and admits no intervening whole-group normal subgroup. Finite groups have both, by repeatedly choosing maximal permissible terms.

Jordan–Hölder says the multiset of composition factors is independent of the series. Refine two series using intersections and products; the butterfly lemma identifies the factors. A minimal normal subgroup of a finite group is a direct product of isomorphic simple groups, so each chief factor has that form.

For $A_4$, the chief series $1<V_4<A_4$ has an elementary abelian factor of order four. A composition series inserts an order-two subgroup of $V_4$ and has factors $C_2,C_2,C_3$. That inserted subgroup is not normal in $A_4$.

explanation: Every noncentral conjugacy class has size divisible by $p$. The identity is central, so the center cannot have size zero and must have at least $p$ elements. A simple finite $p$-group is therefore exactly a cyclic group of prime order.
intuition: A group whose order is a prime power has enough central structure to start an inductive decomposition.
pitfall: A nontrivial center does not imply that the whole $p$-group is abelian. $D_{4}$ and $Q_{8}$ are nonabelian 2-groups.
prompt: Use the class equation for $D_{4}$ or $Q_{8}$ and locate the central involution.
proof: In the class equation, noncentral class sizes are indices of proper centralizers and hence positive powers of $p$. Thus $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$. If $G$ is simple its nontrivial center must be $G$, making it abelian; a finite simple abelian group has prime order.

reading.title: Centers, maximal subgroups and the Frattini argument
paragraphs: The class equation modulo $p$ proves that a nontrivial normal subgroup of a finite $p$-group meets the center nontrivially. Also $G/Z(G)$ cyclic implies $G$ abelian: representatives are powers of one element times central elements.

Every proper subgroup of a finite $p$-group is properly contained in its normalizer. A maximal subgroup is therefore normal and has index $p$. For an abelian $p$-group, splitting off suitable cyclic factors proves the cyclic prime-power decomposition.

If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $P$ is Sylow in $N$, conjugation by any $g\in G$ produces another Sylow subgroup of $N$. Conjugacy inside $N$ gives $G=N_G(P)N$, the Frattini argument. It links local Sylow information to global normal structure.

reading.title: The two nonabelian groups of odd prime-cube order
paragraphs: For odd $p$, the two nonabelian groups of order $p^3$ are the upper unitriangular $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb F_p$, of exponent $p$, and $C_{p^2}\rtimes C_p$, where the acting generator sends $a$ to $a^{1+p}$. The abelian possibilities are $C_{p^3}$, $C_{p^2}\times C_p$ and $C_p^3$.

In class two, commutators are central, so collection formulas reduce powers of products to powers of their factors and a binomial commutator correction. This distinguishes the two exponent cases. At $p=2$ the nonabelian possibilities are instead the dihedral and quaternion groups of order eight.

The Frattini subgroup $\Phi(P)=P^{\prime}P^p$ records nongenerators; a set generates $P$ exactly when its images span $P/\Phi(P)$ over $\mathbb F_p$. This quotient turns a generating-set question into linear algebra.

definition: |\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)|=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(p^n-p^i),\qquad U_n(\mathbb F_p)=\{I+A:A\text{ strictly upper triangular}\}
explanation: The first column can be any nonzero vector; each later column must avoid the span of its predecessors. In the unitriangular subgroup there are $n(n-1)/2$ arbitrary entries above the diagonal. It captures the entire $p$-part of the general linear group order. Every finite $p$-group $G$ embeds into $U_|G|(F_p)$, although this construction can use a much larger dimension than necessary.
intuition: An invertible matrix is an ordered basis. Counting successive independent columns counts the finite general linear group.
pitfall: Matrix entries and determinants are computed in the finite field, not over the reals. A discrete finite-field matrix grid is not a continuous geometric surface.
prompt: Count $\operatorname{GL}_{2}(F_{2})=6$ and its upper-unitriangular subgroup of order 2. Then compare with $S_{3}$.
proof: For column $i+1$, the span of the preceding independent columns has $p^i$ vectors, leaving $p^n-p^i$ choices. Factoring out $p^i$ from each factor gives total $p$-exponent $0+1+$⋯+($n-1$). Unitriangular matrices have exactly that many free field entries and form a subgroup. For the embedding claim, Cayley's theorem gives a faithful permutation-matrix representation over $F_p$; every $p$-subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F_p)$ lies in a conjugate of its unitriangular Sylow $p$-subgroup.

title: Flags: a line inside a plane

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §5 Parabolic Subgroups: complete flags and flag stabilizers

intuition: A flag remembers a sequence of nested directions. In three dimensions, preserve a line and then the plane containing it; this forces a triangular pattern in the matrix.
explanation: We use column vectors and left actions throughout. Preserving the first line forces the first column to have only its first entry nonzero. Preserving the first plane forces the third entry of the second column to vanish. Invertibility then makes every diagonal entry nonzero. A partial flag omits some intermediate dimensions; its stabilizer is a parabolic subgroup.
theorem: B=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\0&d&e\\0&0&f\end{pmatrix}:adf\ne0\right\},\qquad \mathrm{GL}_3(F)/B\cong\{\text{complete flags in }F^3\}\quad\text{as sets with an action}.
proof: The column conditions are exactly preservation of each subspace in the standard flag. Every complete flag admits an adapted basis; the matrix with this basis as columns sends the standard flag to it, so the action is transitive. The map $gB \mapsto  g\cdot F_{0}$ is a well-defined equivariant bijection by the stabilizer criterion.
pitfall: This coset space is a set with a GL action, not generally a quotient group: $B$ need not be normal. For row/right conventions the triangular pattern must be translated consistently.
prompt: Follow the nested subspaces and ask which entries of a column-action matrix must vanish at each stage.

reading.title: Borel, parabolic and Levi structure
paragraphs: For a standard complete flag, its stabilizer is $B=U\rtimes T$, with $U$ upper unitriangular and $T$ invertible diagonal. A partial flag has a block upper triangular stabilizer $P=U_P\rtimes L_P$; its Levi factor is block diagonal and its unipotent radical has identity diagonal blocks.

The only subspaces invariant under the entire standard Borel are the initial coordinate subspaces. The parabolic subgroups containing that Borel are the corresponding staircase groups. The normalizer identity $P=N_G(U_P)$ recovers the parabolic from its unipotent radical.

Kolchin’s theorem says a subgroup consisting entirely of unipotent matrices has a common invariant complete flag, hence is conjugate into the upper unitriangular group. Its key step is a common fixed nonzero vector; quotient by that line and induct. This is stronger than triangularising each element separately.

title: Schur: maps between irreducible worlds

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: An equivariant map cannot carve a nontrivial invariant piece out of an irreducible representation. It either loses everything or identifies the whole representation with another.
explanation: Let $V$ and $W$ be nonzero irreducible modules. The kernel and image of an equivariant map are invariant subspaces. Irreducibility therefore leaves only two possibilities for each. Over the complex numbers, finite dimension gives the stronger scalar-endomorphism statement, since an endomorphism has an eigenvalue.
theorem: T\ne0\Longrightarrow T:V\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}W,\qquad \operatorname{End}_G(V)=\mathbb C I_V\quad(V\text{ irreducible, finite-dimensional over }\mathbb C).
proof: If $T$ is nonzero then its kernel cannot be all of $V$ and its image cannot be zero; irreducibility gives ker $T=0$ and im $T=W$. For a complex equivariant endomorphism choose an eigenvalue $\lambda$. The map $T-\lambda I$ is equivariant and has a nonzero kernel; the first statement forces $T-\lambda I=0$.
pitfall: The scalar conclusion need not hold over the real numbers. Nonzero vector spaces are required in the definition of irreducibility.
prompt: Compare a nonzero map between irreducible modules with a projection from a reducible module. Which invariant kernel is permitted?

title: Orthogonality turns traces into multiplicities

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example

intuition: Irreducible characters act like perpendicular measuring directions. Weight each conjugacy class by its size, take an inner product, and the result tells you how many copies of an irreducible representation are present.
explanation: Let $G$ be finite and all representations finite-dimensional over the complex numbers; $\chi ^{i}$ are its irreducible characters. For $S_{3}$ the conjugacy classes have sizes 1, 3 and 2, represented by the identity, a transposition and a three-cycle. In this order the irreducible characters are (1,1,1), ($1,-1,1$) and ($2,0,-1$). Their dimensions satisfy $1^{2}+1^{2}+2^{2}=6$. The square of the standard character is (4,0,1), so the tensor square contains one copy of each irreducible.
proof: Proof idea for orthogonality: average the group action on Hom(V,W) to project onto equivariant maps. Its trace is the character inner product. Schur’s lemma makes this dimension 1 for equal irreducibles and 0 for distinct ones. Additivity gives the multiplicity formula. For the displayed tensor square, all three weighted inner products are 1, and the dimensions sum to 4.
pitfall: Do not take an unweighted dot product of table rows. Complex conjugation is part of the inner product, even when every entry in this particular table is real.
prompt: Select two $S_{3}$ irreducibles to tensor. Check every multiplicity with weights 1, 3, 2 and verify the total dimension.

reading.title: Orthogonality and reading normal structure
paragraphs: The irreducible rows are orthonormal for $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=|G|^{-1}\sum_C|C|\alpha(C)\overline{\beta(C)}$. Column orthogonality gives $\sum_i\chi_i(g)\overline{\chi_i(h)}=0$ for nonconjugate elements and $|C_G(g)|$ for equal classes. A character decomposes with nonnegative integer coefficients obtained from row inner products.

Twisting an irreducible by a linear character preserves irreducibility. Virtual characters allow integer coefficients, and norm one means an irreducible character or its negative. For an actual character, norms one, two and three force a sum of that many distinct irreducibles; the restriction on the norm matters.

The kernel of a character consists of classes where $\chi(g)=\chi(1)$. Every normal subgroup is an intersection of irreducible kernels. Characters of $G/N$ are exactly the irreducibles whose kernels contain $N$. The scalar sets $Z_\chi=\{g:|\chi(g)|=\chi(1)\}$ recover the center by intersection, and successive quotient tables detect nilpotence. The normal-subgroup data also determines solvability.

reading.title: Nine character-table constructions
paragraphs: For $C_n$, all irreducibles are $\chi_j(g^k)=e^{2\pi ijk/n}$. For a direct product, multiply one irreducible character from each factor. Thus every finite abelian group has only linear irreducibles. A permutation character counts fixed points; its inner product with the trivial character counts orbits. Linear characters factor through the abelianization.

For $S_3$, class sizes $1,3,2$ yield rows $(1,1,1)$, $(1,-1,1)$ and $(2,0,-1)$. For $S_4$, use its quotient $S_3$, the permutation module minus the trivial line, and the sign twist; the degrees are $1,1,2,3,3$.

The two nonabelian groups of order eight have the same ordinary character table: four linear rows and a degree-two row $(2,-2,0,0,0)$ with the central classes first. The table alone therefore does not identify the group. For $A_5$, orthogonality gives degrees $1,3,3,4,5$ and the golden-ratio entries on the two five-cycle classes.

reading.title: Practice routes: dihedral, symmetric and quotient tables
paragraphs: For the dihedral group of order $2n$, the degree-two rows have rotation values $2\cos(2\pi jk/n)$ and zero reflection values. Separate the even and odd cases: the number of linear characters changes because the abelianization changes.

To build the table of $S_5$, organize columns by cycle partitions, start with trivial and sign, use the degree-four standard representation and its sign twist, then construct exterior and symmetric squares and subtract known constituents. The final degrees are $1,1,4,4,5,5,6$, whose squares sum to $120$.

For quotient exercises, first identify which rows contain the chosen normal subgroup in their kernel, then merge the appropriate quotient classes. Check dimensions, weighted row norms and column centralizer sizes after every construction.

title: Induction: one copy over every coset

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: A representation of a subgroup describes local symmetry. Induction places a copy of that vector space over each left coset and lets the whole group move the copies, applying a subgroup action whenever the coset representative changes.
explanation: Let $G$ be finite, $H\le G$, $F$ a field, and $W$ a finite-dimensional left $FH$-module. Choose representatives $t$ for the left cosets $tH$. The tensor relation $th\otimes w=t\otimes hw$ ensures that changing representatives is consistent. The coset copies generally are not $G$-invariant: the group permutes them.
proof: As a right $FH$-module, $FG=\bigoplus_{t\in T}tFH$ for a left transversal $T$. Tensoring with $W$ gives $FG\otimes_{FH}W\cong\bigoplus_{t\in T}t\otimes W$ as vector spaces. Hence the dimension is $[G:H]\dim_F W$. For the trivial $H$-module the induced action permutes the cosets.
pitfall: Restriction keeps the vector space and uses fewer group elements; induction usually enlarges the vector space. The direct sum over cosets is a vector-space decomposition, not a decomposition into $G$-submodules.
prompt: For $H=S_{2}$ inside $S_{3}$, follow the three cosets. Inducing the trivial $H$ representation gives the three-point permutation representation.
subject: Modules & representations

reading.title: Coset blocks and the induced character formula
paragraphs: For $H\le G$, induction is $FG\otimes_{FH}V$. A left-coset transversal decomposes it as a direct sum of copies $t\otimes V$, giving dimension $[G:H]\dim V$. The action permutes these blocks and applies an $H$-matrix whenever a block maps to itself.
Taking traces gives $\chi^G(g)=|H|^{-1}\sum_{x\in G,\ x^{-1}gx\in H}\chi(x^{-1}gx)$. Regrouping by $H$-conjugacy classes weights the terms by centralizer ratios. A class missing $H$ contributes zero.

The adjunction sends a map $V\to\operatorname{Res}_H^G U$ to $g\otimes v\mapsto g f(v)$; evaluate at $1\otimes v$ for the inverse. Over $\mathbb C$ this becomes equality of the corresponding character inner products. It explains decomposition multiplicities without constructing every induced matrix.

reading.title: From a Borel subgroup to all representations of a linear group
paragraphs: For $G=\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_q)$, conjugacy types are scalar, nontrivial Jordan, split semisimple with distinct eigenvalues, and nonsplit semisimple. Their centralizer orders are respectively $|G|$, $q(q-1)$, $(q-1)^2$ and $q^2-1$. These determine class sizes.

There are $q-1$ determinant characters of degree one and $q-1$ Steinberg twists of degree $q$. Inducing a diagonal character from the Borel with distinct multiplicative characters gives a principal-series irreducible of degree $q+1$; interchanging the two characters gives the same representation. There are $(q-1)(q-2)/2$ such representations.

The remaining cuspidal representations have degree $q-1$ and are indexed by Frobenius orbits of characters of $\mathbb F_{q^2}^\times$ not fixed by Frobenius. Their number is $q(q-1)/2$. Summing all four families gives $q^2-1$ irreducibles, and summing their squared degrees gives $|G|=q(q-1)^2(q+1)$.

The construction uses restriction, induction, orthogonality and the nonsplit torus together; counting degrees alone does not prove existence or irreducibility. The linked exercises give the class-value calculations and virtual-character construction.

title: Frobenius reciprocity: extend or restrict

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: To define a group-compatible map out of an induced representation, it is enough to define it on the original subgroup copy. The rest is forced by symmetry.
explanation: The Hom-space statement works over any field. Given an $H$-equivariant map $f$ from $W$ to the restricted module $V$, extend it by $a\otimes w\mapsto a\cdot f(w)$. Conversely evaluate a $G$-equivariant map on $1\otimes w$. Over the complex numbers for finite groups, taking dimensions gives the familiar equality of character multiplicities.
proof: The extension is well-defined because $ah\otimes w=a\otimes hw$ and $H$-equivariance gives $ah\cdot f(w)=a\cdot f(hw)$. It is $G$-equivariant by construction. Evaluation at $1\otimes w$ reverses this operation, so the maps are inverse linear isomorphisms. The character formula follows by identifying character inner products with dimensions of equivariant Hom-spaces.
pitfall: Reciprocity relates the multiplicity of a chosen irreducible after induction to its multiplicity after restriction. It does not assert that induction and restriction undo one another.
prompt: For $G=S_3$ and $H=\langle(12)\rangle$, the standard representation restricts to $\mathbf1_H\oplus\operatorname{sgn}_H$. Deduce that $\operatorname{Ind}_H^{S_3}\mathbf1_H\cong\mathbf1\oplus\operatorname{Std}$.

title: A representation is a linear group action

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7
source.section: Chapter 4, Definition 4.2 and Theorem 4.4; left-action convention here

intuition: A group can move a finite set; a representation moves vectors while respecting addition and scalar multiplication. Choosing a basis turns the action into matrices, without changing the underlying action.
explanation: This companion uses column vectors and left actions. James–Liebeck uses row vectors and right actions; translate conventions before comparing matrix products. A linear action automatically gives invertible maps because the action of $g^{-1}$ reverses the action of $g$. A representation is faithful when only the identity acts as the identity on every vector.
proof: The homomorphism equation gives the action law by applying both sides to $v$, and $\rho (e)=I$ gives the identity law. Conversely a linear action defines linear maps $\rho (g)$; the inverse action makes them invertible and the action law makes $\rho$ a homomorphism. Its kernel records exactly those group elements invisible to the action.
pitfall: One vector being fixed does not mean a group element lies in the kernel. It must fix every vector. With column vectors the rightmost matrix acts first.
prompt: Move a vector and the coordinate frame under a permutation. Compare composing the matrices with composing the corresponding actions.

title: Turn a finite action into a vector space

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7
source.section: Chapter 4, Definition 4.10; Example 4.11. The source uses right actions; this site uses left actions.

intuition: Replace each point of a finite $G$-set by an independent basis vector. A group element now moves labels and also moves any linear combination of labels.
explanation: The action on the basis extends uniquely by linearity. This separates the geometric object from the vector space built from its features. The cube’s eight vertices produce an eight-dimensional permutation representation, whereas its ordinary spatial action is three-dimensional. Different feature sets therefore reveal different representations of the same group.
proof: Both sides send $e_{x}$ to e_(ghx), so they agree on a basis. A permutation matrix has a 1 in the diagonal entry indexed by $x$ exactly when $gx=x$, giving the trace formula. The kernel of the permutation representation equals the kernel of the action on $X$ because basis vectors remain distinct.
pitfall: A drawing of three axes does not display an eight-dimensional representation faithfully as a geometric embedding. It can display its basis permutation and matrix exactly.
prompt: In the three-point example, follow a coefficient attached to one basis vector. Then compare the cube actions on vertices, edges, faces and diagonals.

title: A hidden line and a hidden plane

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7

intuition: Permuting three coordinates leaves their average unchanged. It also keeps zero-sum fluctuations at zero sum. These are two independent parts of the same representation.
explanation: For the permutation action of $S_{3}$ on $R^{3}$, $L$ is a trivial subrepresentation and $W$ is the standard representation. A submodule must be both a vector subspace and stable under every group element. A basis adapted to $L$ and $W$ makes every action matrix block diagonal. The analogous complex decomposition uses $C^{3}$, the same constant line and the complex sum-zero plane.
proof: Permutations fix (1,1,1) and preserve the sum of coordinates, hence preserve $L$ and $W$. Every vector has the displayed decomposition. If a constant vector has zero sum, its constant is zero over $R$ or $C$, so $L\cap W=0$ and the decomposition is unique.
pitfall: Stability under one group element is not stability under the whole group unless that element generates it. Over a field of characteristic 3, the constant line lies inside the sum-zero subspace and this particular direct-sum formula fails.
prompt: Change the vector coordinates and apply different permutations. Its mean stays fixed; subtracting that mean leaves a vector in the invariant sum-zero plane.

title: The group algebra: add symmetries

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7

intuition: The group law lets you compose symmetries; the group algebra also lets you take weighted sums of them. Its basis vectors are group elements, and multiplication extends the original group law linearly.
definition: FG=\left\{\sum_{g\in G}a_g g:a_g\in F\right\},\qquad \left(\sum_g a_g g\right)\left(\sum_h b_h h\right)=\sum_{g,h}a_gb_h(gh).
explanation: Here $G$ is finite and $F$ is a field, so $FG$ has dimension $|G|$. A group representation extends to an algebra action by sending a weighted sum of group elements to the same weighted sum of their matrices. The regular left action permutes the basis $G$ by left multiplication. General algebra elements need not act invertibly.
proof: Expand both a and $b$ in the group basis. Bilinearity and $\rho (gh)=\rho (g)\rho (h)$ make the two products equal term by term. Conversely, a unital $FG$-module restricts to a $G$-action since the basis elements $g$ and $g^{-1}$ act as inverse operators.
pitfall: A group element $g$ is a basis vector in FG, not a scalar in $F$. The zero algebra element cannot act invertibly on a nonzero module.
prompt: Follow how group multiplication determines products of basis elements, then how linear extension produces an action of a weighted sum.

title: The same symmetry in different coordinates

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7

intuition: An intertwiner translates vectors between two representations without changing what any group action means. Acting then translating must equal translating then acting.
explanation: An invertible intertwiner identifies two representations. Their matrices may look different because the bases differ, while their actions have the same algebraic structure. Noninvertible intertwiners also matter: invariant kernels, invariant images and equivariant projections identify meaningful pieces.
theorem: T\text{ invertible}\Longrightarrow \rho_W(g)=T\rho_V(g)T^{-1},\qquad \ker T\le V,\ \operatorname{im}T\le W\text{ invariant}.
proof: For $v$ in ker $T$, equivariance gives $T\rho _V(g)v=\rho _W(g)Tv=0$. For $w=Tv$ in the image, $\rho _W(g)w=T\rho _V(g)v$ remains in the image. If $T$ is invertible, rearranging the intertwining equation gives simultaneous conjugacy for every $g$.
pitfall: A different conjugating matrix for each group element does not establish equivalence. One fixed invertible $T$ must work for the entire group.
prompt: Compare a vector written in the standard coordinates with its constant-line and sum-zero components. Check that this one change of basis works for every permutation.

title: Restriction to a cycle reveals eigenvalues

source.title: Etingof et al. · Introduction to Representation Theory
source.section: §3.3, complex characters of cyclic groups; original eigenvector calculation

intuition: If the only allowed symmetry is repeated application of one finite-order transformation, each complex eigendirection evolves by a single root of unity. Restriction turns the representation into independent cyclic modes.
explanation: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex representation and $r$ an element of finite order $m$. On $V\lambda$ every power $r^{k}$ acts by $\lambda ^{k}$; its dimension is the multiplicity of that one-dimensional cyclic representation. In the natural three-dimensional cube representation, a quarter-turn about the vertical axis has eigenvalues 1, $i$ and $-i$. The real horizontal plane splits into two lines only after complexification.
proof: The relation $\rho (r)^m=I$ makes its minimal polynomial divide $X^m-1$. Over $C$ that polynomial splits with distinct roots, so $\rho (r)$ is diagonalizable. Every eigenspace is stable under all powers of $\rho (r)$, on which they act as the corresponding powers of its eigenvalue. Choosing a basis of each eigenspace gives the decomposition and trace formula.
pitfall: A group of order four has four complex irreducible characters, but a particular representation need not contain all four. For the natural cube quarter-turn the multiplicities are 1, 1, 0, 1 at 1, $i$, $-1$, $-i$.
prompt: Compare the real invariant plane with the complex eigenvalues of a quarter-turn. Verify the character values ($3,1,-1,1$) on $e,r,r^{2},r^{3}$.

title: Why the cube has 48 symmetries

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: A symmetry sends each positive coordinate axis to one of six face directions. Once its three images are chosen orthogonally, every vertex has a determined destination.
definition: C=[-1,1]^3,\qquad G=\{Q\in O(3):Q(C)=C\}.\quad Qe_j=\varepsilon_j e_{\sigma(j)},\quad\sigma\in S_3,\ \varepsilon_j\in\{\pm1\}.
explanation: Centre the cube at the origin. Its six face centres are $\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3$. A symmetry permutes these centres, so its matrix has one nonzero entry in each row and column, equal to $+1$ or $-1$. Conversely, every such signed permutation preserves the inequalities $|x_i|\le1$ defining the solid cube.
proof: Choose the underlying permutation in 6 ways and the three signs in 8 ways; these choices give distinct matrices. The determinant is $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma )\varepsilon _{1}\varepsilon _{2}\varepsilon _{3}$. For each permutation, exactly four sign choices give $determinant +1$ and four give $-1$.
pitfall: 48 counts all Euclidean symmetries of the cube, including orientation reversal. Physical rotations alone give 24. The camera position does not change which matrix the cube represents.
prompt: Keep the coordinate permutation fixed and flip one sign. Which vertices move, and how does the determinant change?

title: A symmetry as a word of motions

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: Two quarter turns can build every rotational symmetry. A word records how the final symmetry was made, while its matrix records the resulting linear map.
explanation: A is a positive quarter turn about the x-axis; $B$ is a positive quarter turn about the z-axis. Vectors are columns. In a product AB, $B$ acts first. If the controls apply A, then $B$, then J, the displayed product must be JBA. Different words can represent the same group element; a breadth-first search produces a shortest word in a specified generator alphabet.
theorem: G^+=\langle A,B\rangle,\quad G=\langle A,B,J\rangle,\quad A^4=B^4=J^2=I,\quad AB\ne BA.
proof: The group generated by A and $B$ sends $e_{3}$ to all six face directions. The stabilizer of $e_{3}$ contains $I$, $B$, $B^{2}$, $B^{3}$. Orbit–stabilizer gives at least 24 elements, and all generated matrices lie among the 24 rotations, so equality holds. Adjoining $-I$ gives the other determinant component. For noncommutativity, AB $e_{1}=e_{3}$ but BA $e_{1}=e_{2}$.
pitfall: A relation such as $A^{4}=I$ does not say these are all the defining relations. A shortest word is relative to the allowed alphabet and need not be unique.
prompt: Apply A then $B$; reset and apply $B$ then A. Track the same colored vertex, then compare the unsimplified matrix products.

title: One cube, four actions

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: Changing what you label changes what a symmetry can be observed to do. Vertices, edges, faces, and diagonal lines are four different sets on which the same group acts.
explanation: For vertices, apply $Q$ to the point. For an edge, apply $Q$ to its unordered endpoint pair. For a face, apply $Q$ to its outward unit normal. For a body diagonal, apply $Q$ to the line through an opposite vertex pair; vectors $v$ and $-v$ represent the same diagonal. Each construction respects composition, so each gives a group homomorphism.
proof: Fixing every vertex fixes three independent vectors. Fixing every face fixes the three positive coordinate normals. Fixing every edge fixes each vertex, which is the intersection of its three incident edges. On diagonal lines, $-I$ is invisible. If $Q$ fixes all four lines, write $Qd_i=\varepsilon_i d_i$ with $\varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}$. Distinct diagonal representatives have nonzero dot products. Orthogonality forces $\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j=1$, so all signs agree. Three independent representatives then give $Q=\pm I$.
pitfall: A body diagonal is an unoriented line in this action. Treating its two endpoints as separate labels changes the action and its kernel.
prompt: Apply $J=-I$. Compare the induced permutations in all four views. Which view loses information?

title: Count symmetries by fixing one object

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: First choose where one marked object goes. Then count how much freedom remains after its destination has been fixed.
definition: G_x=\{g\in G:g\cdot x=x\},\qquad G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\},\qquad |G|=|G\cdot x|\,|G_x|.
explanation: Both the rotational and full cube groups act transitively on each of the four object sets. In the rotational group, the stabilizer orders are 3 for a vertex, 2 for an edge, 4 for a face, and 6 for an unoriented diagonal. In the full group these become 6, 4, 8, and 12 respectively. A diagonal stabilizer may exchange its two endpoints.
proof: The map from left cosets $gG_{x}$ to orbit points g·x is well-defined and bijective: $g\cdot x=h\cdot x$ exactly when $h^{-1}g\in G_{x}$. Thus the orbit has index [$G$:$G_{x}]$. The cube actions are transitive, and substituting their sizes gives the listed stabilizer orders.
pitfall: Fixing an edge setwise allows its endpoints to swap. Fixing a face setwise does not require its four vertices to remain individually fixed.
prompt: Select one face and show only its stabilizer. Use its four rotations to explain the factorization $24=6\times 4$.

title: Why cube rotations are S₄

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: Four diagonal lines look too sparse to record a three-dimensional motion. For rotations, however, their permutation remembers the entire motion.
explanation: Use representatives $d_{1}=(1,1,1)$, $d_{2}=(1,1,-1)$, $d_{3}=(1,-1,1)$, $d_{4}=(-1,1,1)$. Our generators induce $A=(1$ 3 4 2) and $B=(1$ 4 2 3), with the same rightmost-first composition convention as the matrices. This correspondence translates spatial composition into permutation multiplication.
proof: The kernel of the full action on diagonal lines is $\{I,-I\}$. Intersect it with the rotations: only $I$ remains, since $\det(-I_3)=-1$. The action therefore injects the rotation group, of order $24$, into $S_4$, also of order $24$. It is an isomorphism.
pitfall: The full 48-element cube group is not $S_{4}$. Its diagonal action is two-to-one. Also, geometric $determinant +1$ does not imply that the induced diagonal permutation is even.
prompt: Choose a quarter turn. Its spatial determinant $is +1$; what is the sign of its 4-cycle on diagonal lines?

title: Separate rotation from central inversion

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: Every full cube symmetry has a unique rotational part and one extra yes-or-no choice: whether to invert all three coordinates.
explanation: If det $Q=+1$, take $\varepsilon =0$ and $R=Q$. If det $Q=-1$, take $\varepsilon =1$ and $R=-Q$. Central inversion commutes with every linear map. Its only overlap with the rotation group is the identity. These facts make the decomposition a direct product, stronger than merely splitting the set into two equal halves.
theorem: G\cong G^+\times C_2\cong S_4\times C_2,\qquad Q\longmapsto\bigl(\phi_D(Q),\det Q\bigr).
proof: Let $J=-I_3$. The map $(R,\varepsilon)\mapsto J^\varepsilon R$ from $G^+\times C_2$ to $G$ is a homomorphism because $J$ is central. Every element of determinant $-1$ is $J$ times a rotation, proving surjectivity. Since $G^+\cap\{I,J\}=\{I\}$, the map is injective. Thus $G\cong S_4\times C_2$.
pitfall: The determinant character on $G$ is not the sign of its diagonal permutation. The two coordinates of $S_{4}\times C_{2}$ record different information.
prompt: Hold the diagonal permutation fixed and toggle J. Observe which object actions change and why the rotation/inversion pair remains unique.

title: Orthogonality preserves geometry

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: An orthogonal matrix moves an orthonormal frame to another orthonormal frame. It preserves lengths and angles while possibly reversing handedness.
definition: O(n)=\{Q\in M_n(\mathbb R):Q^TQ=I\},\qquad SO(n)=\{Q\in O(n):\det Q=1\}.
explanation: The equation $Q^{T}Q=I$ means the columns form an orthonormal basis. It gives ($Qu)\cdot (Qv)=u\cdot v$ for every pair of vectors. Determinant separates the two possible orientations. A reflection in the plane perpendicular to a unit vector $n$ has matrix $H_{n}=I-2nn^{T}$. In three dimensions, central inversion $-I$ reverses orientation but is not a plane reflection.
proof: Taking determinants in $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I$ gives $(\det Q)^2=1$. Determinant is multiplicative. For a unit vector $n$, the reflection $H_n=I-2nn^{\mathsf T}$ fixes $n^\perp$ pointwise and sends $n$ to $-n$, so its determinant is $-1$. In contrast, $-I_3$ fixes no nonzero vector. Along a continuous path in $O(n)$ the determinant is constant, since it takes values in the discrete set $\{1,-1\}$.
pitfall: An animation from $I$ to an orientation-reversing matrix cannot remain a continuous path of orthogonal matrices. A morph that collapses the cube is an illustration, not a rigid motion.
prompt: Compare a plane reflection with central inversion. Display each fixed subspace and the determinant.

title: The circle group and its reflections

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: Plane rotations add angles. Adding a reflection creates a second component that reverses the direction in which angles compose.
explanation: Every element of SO(2) is exactly one $R\theta$ modulo $2\pi$. Every determinant $-1$ element of O(2) is $R\theta F$. It is reflection in the line making angle $\theta /2$ with the x-axis. The relation $FR\theta F=R-\theta$ explains why O(2) is noncommutative although SO(2) is commutative. Restricting $\theta$ to multiples of $2\pi /n$ recovers the rotational and full symmetry groups of a regular n-gon.
theorem: SO(2)\cong\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z),\qquad O(2)\cong SO(2)\rtimes C_2,\qquad FR_\theta F=R_{-\theta}.
proof: The first column is $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^{\mathsf T}$. The perpendicular unit second column is either $(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)^{\mathsf T}$ or its negative. These give $R_\theta$ and $R_\theta F$. Matrix multiplication proves angle addition and $FR_\theta F=R_{-\theta}$. Every orthogonal matrix has exactly one of the two forms, so $O(2)\cong SO(2)\rtimes C_2$.
pitfall: $R\theta F$ is reflection through angle $\theta /2$, not $\theta$. The semidirect product is not a direct product: reflection generally does not commute with rotation.
prompt: Compare $FR\theta$ with $R\theta F$ while increasing $\theta$. At which angles do the two transformations coincide?

title: SO(3): an axis and a turning angle

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: A three-dimensional rotation leaves an axis fixed and rotates its perpendicular plane. The cube rotation group selects just 24 points from this continuous family.
explanation: Rodrigues’ formula separates a vector into its component along $n$ and its component perpendicular to $n$. The first stays fixed; the second undergoes a plane rotation. Every element of SO(3) has this form. Choose $0\le \theta \le \pi$: a nonidentity rotation determines an axis line, but at $\theta =\pi$ the choices $n$ and $-n$ give the same matrix. At $\theta =0$ every axis gives the identity.
proof: A real orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix has eigenvalues of modulus one and nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. Determinant +1 forces at least one eigenvalue +1. Its unit eigenvector $n$ has an invariant orthogonal complement, where the restriction has $determinant +1$ and hence is a plane rotation. Decomposing into $n$ and $n$⊥ gives Rodrigues’ formula and the trace identity.
pitfall: The trace determines the angle in [$0,\pi ]$ but not the axis. Generic SO(3) rotations do not preserve the cube. Linear interpolation of rotation matrices is generally not orthogonal.
prompt: Rotate about a body diagonal continuously. Which angle values return the cube to its original set of occupied points?

title: Invariant subspaces are persistent patterns

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original examples
source.section: §§1.3, 1.7: representations, invariant subspaces and group algebras

intuition: A pattern of weights is an invariant mode when every allowed symmetry keeps it inside the same family of patterns. The individual vector may move; the family survives.
definition: W\le V\text{ is }G\text{-invariant}\iff\rho(g)W\subseteq W\quad(\forall g\in G).
explanation: Label the square vertices cyclically and let its symmetries permute coordinates in $\mathbb R^4$. The pieces are $T=\operatorname{span}(1,1,1,1)$, $L=\operatorname{span}(1,-1,1,-1)$ and $U=\{(a,b,-a,-b):a,b\in\mathbb R\}$. The constant pattern is fixed, the alternating pattern can change sign, and opposite-vertex contrasts move within a plane. Stability of the whole subspace is the point.
theorem: \mathbb R^4=T\oplus L\oplus U,\qquad\dim T=1,\quad\dim L=1,\quad\dim U=2.
proof: A quarter turn and the reflection $i\mapsto -i$ generate the square group. Their coordinate permutations preserve $T$, $L$, and $U$ by direct substitution. These three spaces are pairwise orthogonal for the standard dot product, and their dimensions sum to 4, proving the direct sum. The quarter turn acts on $U$ as a 90° plane rotation, which has no invariant real line; hence $U$ is irreducible over $\mathbb R$.
pitfall: Invariant means stable as a subspace under every group element. It does not mean every vector is fixed, and stability under one chosen symmetry alone is insufficient.
prompt: Choose a vector with four vertex weights. Decompose it into constant, alternating, and opposite-contrast parts, then apply a quarter turn.

title: Irreducibility depends on the field

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original examples
source.section: §§1.3, 1.7: representations, invariant subspaces and group algebras

intuition: A real rotation has no real eigenline unless its angle is 0 or $\pi$. Over the complex numbers, the same matrix splits into two one-dimensional eigenmodes.
explanation: A rotation through $120^\circ$ on $\mathbb R^2$ has no invariant real line, so it is irreducible. After extending scalars to $\mathbb C$, the eigenvalues are $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $\omega^{-1}$, giving two invariant complex lines. Complex eigenvectors are represented by real and imaginary parts, not by extra lines in the original real plane.
theorem: \mathbb R^2\text{ is irreducible over }\mathbb R,\qquad\mathbb C^2=E_\omega\oplus E_{\omega^{-1}},\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}.
proof: The characteristic polynomial is $t^{2}+t+1$, whose discriminant is $-3$; hence there is no real eigenvalue or real invariant line. Over $\mathbb C$ it has the two distinct roots $\omega$ and $\omega ^{-1}$. Their eigenspaces are one-dimensional, invariant under the generator, and therefore invariant under all of $C_{3}$.
pitfall: “Every irreducible representation of an abelian group is one-dimensional” requires hypotheses such as finite-dimensional representations over an algebraically closed field. It is false over $\mathbb R$ as stated.
prompt: Inspect the fixed real axis, the real rotation plane and the two complex eigenvalues. Which complex eigenlines have no real counterpart?

title: Average to reveal invariant complements

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory

intuition: A random projection onto an invariant subspace may favor one viewpoint. Averaging all its symmetry-transformed versions removes that preference.
explanation: Let $V$ be finite-dimensional and $W$ a $G$-invariant subspace. Choose any linear projection $P$ onto $W$. The averaged map $P_G$ still projects onto $W$ and now commutes with the whole action. Its kernel gives an invariant complementary subspace. Repeating this splitting produces a direct sum of irreducible representations.
proof: Every conjugated projection maps into $W$ and is the identity on $W$, so the average has the same two properties and is idempotent. Conjugating the sum by $\rho (h)$ merely reindexes its terms; hence it commutes with the action. Its kernel is therefore invariant. Finite dimension lets us split recursively until all nonzero summands are irreducible.
pitfall: Dividing by $|G|$ requires it to be invertible in the field. In characteristic $p$, let a generator of $C_p$ act by $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The fixed line is invariant but has no invariant complementary line.
prompt: Select the constant component of a square-weight vector. Compare its mean before and after applying $r$ or $s$; averaging over all eight group elements gives that projection.

references.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

reading.title: Averaging and the modular obstruction
paragraphs: For finite $G$ with $|G|$ invertible in $F$, start with any linear projection $p:V\to W$ onto an invariant subspace. Then $\bar p=|G|^{-1}\sum_g gpg^{-1}$ is an equivariant projection onto $W$. Its kernel is an invariant complement. Repeating gives complete reducibility in finite dimension.

The characteristic condition is also necessary for semisimplicity of $FG$. The augmentation map $\varepsilon:FG\to F$ sends $\sum a_gg$ to $\sum a_g$. Any invariant vector in the regular module is a multiple of $\sum_g g$, whose augmentation is $|G|$. If that is zero in $F$, the trivial quotient cannot have an equivariant section.

title: Characters measure the action economically

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original cube calculations

intuition: A character compresses each matrix to its trace. For a permutation representation this simply counts the labeled objects left in place.
explanation: For complex representations of a finite group, irreducible characters are orthonormal under the class-function inner product, and their inner products with $\chi V$ give multiplicities. The five $S_{4}$ conjugacy classes have cycle types $1^{4}$, $2\cdot 1^{2}$, $2^{2}$, 3·1, and 4. The geometric cube rotation representation has character ($3,-1,-1,0,1$), whereas the zero-sum part of the diagonal permutation representation has character ($3,1,-1,0,-1$). They differ by the sign character.
proof: For a permutation matrix, a diagonal entry equals 1 exactly when that basis object is fixed, proving the fixed-point formula. Trace is unchanged by conjugation, so characters are class functions. Proof idea for the multiplicity formula: average the action on Hom(U,V) to project onto equivariant maps; its trace is the displayed inner product. Complete reducibility and Schur’s lemma identify that dimension with the multiplicity of irreducible $U$.
pitfall: Character values are not always nonnegative or integers. Fixed-point counting applies specifically to permutation representations. Equal dimensions do not imply equivalent representations.
prompt: Compare a face quarter turn in the geometric and diagonal permutation representations. Explain their different traces.

reading.title: What traces remember and how they combine
paragraphs: For a finite group over $\mathbb C$, each matrix of a group element is diagonalizable with roots of unity as eigenvalues. Thus $\chi(g^{-1})=\overline{\chi(g)}$ and $|\chi(g)|\le\chi(1)$. Direct sums add characters; tensor products multiply them; duals conjugate them.

Characters determine semisimple representations up to isomorphism. The irreducible characters form a basis of class functions: the number of irreducibles equals the dimension of the center of $\mathbb CG$, whose class sums form a basis. Also $\sum_i\chi_i(1)^2=|G|$.

Averaging the representation matrices projects onto fixed vectors, so $\dim V^G=|G|^{-1}\sum_g\chi_V(g)$. Apply this to $U^*\otimes V\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)$ to obtain $\langle\chi_U,\chi_V\rangle=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(U,V)$, with the inner-product convention chosen consistently.

reading.title: Character fibers: a useful correction
paragraphs: Equality $\chi(g)=\chi(1)$ forces every eigenvalue to be one, hence $g$ is in the representation kernel. Equality of absolute values means the matrix is scalar. This distinguishes the kernel from the larger scalar preimage.

For a fixed scalar $\lambda\ne1$, the set $\{g:\chi(g)=\lambda\chi(1)\}$ need not be a subgroup: the sign character of $C_2$ with $\lambda=-1$ gives a singleton excluding the identity. Such a fiber is conjugacy-invariant; the fiber at one is the normal kernel. A union of conjugacy classes is not automatically a normal subgroup.

title: Faithful and transitive ask different questions

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: Transitivity asks whether every position is reachable. Faithfulness asks whether every nonidentity symmetry can be detected somewhere. Neither condition forces the other.
explanation: The full cube group on its four diagonal lines is transitive but not faithful: central inversion fixes every line. Its action on the disjoint union of vertices and face centers is faithful but not transitive, because a symmetry preserves each of those two sets. The usual vertex action is both faithful and transitive. Thus reachability and detectability describe independent properties of an action.
proof: An element belongs to the kernel of the homomorphism into $S_X$ exactly when its induced permutation is the identity, which means fixing every point. This gives the intersection formula. The cube examples then establish the claimed distinctions: inversion witnesses a nontrivial diagonal kernel, and vertex faithfulness persists after adjoining a separate orbit of face centers.
pitfall: A transitive action need not be free. The rotation group is transitive on eight vertices but every vertex still has a three-element stabilizer.
prompt: Choose vertices + faces, then follow a vertex and a face. The action is faithful but has two orbits. Compare it with the transitive diagonal action, whose full-group kernel is nontrivial.

title: A stabilizer is local; a kernel is global

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: A stabilizer describes what one chosen object cannot detect. Intersecting stabilizers asks what the entire observation system cannot detect.
explanation: For a transitive action, choose $x$ and set $H=G_{x}$. The action is equivalent to left multiplication on $G/H$. A single stabilizer $H$ need not be normal: moving the chosen object conjugates its stabilizer. The kernel is the largest normal subgroup contained in $H$. In the rotation action on a face, $H$ has order 4 while the kernel is trivial.
theorem: G/H\longrightarrow G\cdot x,\quad gH\longmapsto g\cdot x\quad\text{is a }G\text{-equivariant bijection}.
proof: The coset-to-orbit map is well-defined and bijective by the criterion $h^{-1}g\in H$. An element $a$ fixes every coset exactly when $agH=gH$ for all $g$, equivalently $g^{-1}ag\in H$. Intersect these conditions over $G$. Every normal subgroup contained in $H$ lies in all conjugates of $H$.
pitfall: A nontrivial stabilizer does not mean the action is unfaithful. Kernel elements must fix every object, rather than just the selected one.
prompt: Pick two different faces and compare their stabilizers. Find a rotation in one stabilizer but not the other, then intersect all six.

title: Let a group act on itself in two ways

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: Left multiplication moves every group element uniformly. Conjugation instead changes the frame in which a symmetry is described, preserving its structural type.
explanation: The left regular action is faithful, free, and transitive: any group element can be moved to any other in exactly one way. In the conjugation action, orbits are conjugacy classes, the stabilizer of $x$ is its centralizer $C_G(x)$, and the kernel is the center Z(G). For cube rotations, conjugation carries a rotation axis to the transformed axis while preserving the rotation angle.
proof: For left multiplication, $gx=x$ implies $g=e$, and $yx^{-1}$ carries $x$ to $y$. For conjugation, $gxg^{-1}=x$ is equivalent to $gx=xg$, so the stabilizer is $C_G(x)$. Fixing every element means belonging to $Z(G)$. Orbit–stabilizer now gives $|\operatorname{Cl}(x)|=[G:C_G(x)]$.
pitfall: A left coset and a conjugacy class are different kinds of subsets. Conjugation is not generally transitive, and the identity always forms a singleton orbit.
prompt: Select a quarter turn and conjugate it by different cube symmetries. Track the axis. Then compare the result with ordinary left multiplication.

title: Count cube colorings by fixed colorings

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: Dividing the number of colorings by the group order fails when some colorings have extra symmetry. Burnside’s average automatically accounts for these smaller orbits.
explanation: Color the six faces independently from $k$ labeled colors, allowing repetition and allowing some colors to be unused. A coloring is fixed by a symmetry exactly when it is constant on each cycle of that symmetry’s face permutation. For rotations, the face cycle types and counts are $1^{6}$:1, $1^{2}2^{2}$:3, $1^{2}4$:6, $2^{3}$:6, and $3^{2}$:8. Including orientation reversal gives a different equivalence relation.
proof: Double-count the pairs $(g,c)$ with $g\cdot c=c$. Summing over $g$ gives the sum of fixed-coloring counts. Each orbit contributes $|G|$ pairs by orbit–stabilizer. A coloring fixed by a permutation is constant on each cycle, so a permutation with $r$ cycles fixes $k^r$ colorings. Summing the enumerated cycle types gives the displayed polynomials. Checks: $N_+(2)=N(2)=10$, while $N_+(3)=57$ and $N(3)=56$.
pitfall: These formulas do not require every color to appear. Prescribed color multiplicities need a different fixed-coloring count. Averaging only the 24 improper symmetries is not Burnside’s lemma because they are not a subgroup.
prompt: Use three colors and compare rotations-only with all symmetries. Locate a pair of rotational coloring orbits merged by an orientation-reversing symmetry.

title: Read the same motion through different cycles

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: One quarter turn is simultaneously a permutation of 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces, and 4 diagonal lines. The cycle patterns expose different features of the same motion.
explanation: A face quarter turn has vertex cycle type $4^{2}$, edge type $4^{3}$, face type $1^{2}4$, and diagonal type 4. Its two fixed faces are obvious only in the face view, yet every view detects order four. Central inversion has order two on vertices, edges, and faces but acts identically on the four diagonal lines. An action can hide part or all of an element’s order.
proof: A permutation returns every point to its start exactly when the exponent is divisible by every cycle length, proving the least-common-multiple formula. Restrict $\varphi _X$ to the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$. Its kernel is the displayed intersection, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the order formula. In a faithful action the denominator is one, and every element’s order is preserved.
pitfall: A fixed face in a set action is a face preserved as a whole; its individual points may rotate. The order of an observed permutation equals the group-element order only when the restricted action detects all its powers.
prompt: Compare $B$ and J in all four action views. Recover their orders from cycle lengths and explain the exception for J on diagonals.

title: Elimination reveals a permutation

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: Row operations simplify a matrix, but a permutation records the pivot pattern that triangular operations cannot erase.
definition: B=\{\text{invertible upper triangular matrices}\},\qquad W=\{\text{permutation matrices}\}.
explanation: Work in $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ over a field. Left multiplication performs row operations; right multiplication performs column operations. Allowing only upper triangular operations leaves a unique relative position, indexed by a permutation. These relative positions are the double cosets of $B$. This is the matrix version of comparing two complete flags.
proof: Upper triangular row operations isolate a last nonzero pivot in each successive column. A permutation puts the pivots in standard positions; triangular column operations remove the remaining entries. For uniqueness, triangular transformations preserve the ranks of the appropriate flag intersections, which determine the permutation. This also shows that invertible diagonal matrices and transvections generate the general linear group.
pitfall: The permutation is unique; the two triangular factors usually are not. A double coset is not a quotient group.
prompt: In dimension $2$, compare an upper triangular matrix with one whose lower-left entry is nonzero. They lie in the two different cells.

worked.title: Two cells in dimension two
steps: The identity cell is $B$. The other cell corresponds to the swap matrix and has $q|B|=36$ elements.
The two cells partition $G$: $12+36=48$. Triangular reduction never changes which cell contains the matrix.

reading.title: Counting bases and using elementary matrices
paragraphs: An elementary abelian group of order $p^n$ is an $n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_p$, so its automorphisms form $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)$. Choosing independent columns in order gives $|\operatorname{GL}_n(q)|=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^i)$.

The transvection $X_{ij}(a)=I+aE_{ij}$ adds $a$ times row $j$ to row $i$ under left multiplication. It has determinant one, satisfies $X_{ij}(a)X_{ij}(b)=X_{ij}(a+b)$, and is conjugated by a permutation matrix by relabelling its indices. For distinct indices, the convention $[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ gives $[X_{ij}(a),X_{jk}(b)]=X_{ik}(ab)$.

Elimination reduces an invertible matrix using transvections and invertible diagonal matrices. These generate the general linear group. Restricting which row operations are allowed preserves information about relative flags and exposes the Bruhat permutation.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

reading.title: Existence and uniqueness of the Bruhat cell
paragraphs: Let $B$ be the invertible upper triangular matrices and $W$ the permutation matrices. Then $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB$. Triangular row and column operations yield existence; ranks of intersections between the standard flag and its image determine the permutation uniquely.

For $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ invertible, $c=0$ places the matrix in $B$, while $c\ne0$ places it in the other cell $BsB$. The lower-left entry is the first nontrivial relative-flag invariant. There are two cells, although either cell contains many matrices.

title: Remove the scalar symmetries

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A scalar matrix moves every vector but fixes every line. Projectivising removes exactly that invisible motion.
explanation: For $n\ge2$, the center of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ consists of nonzero scalar matrices; in $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$ they also satisfy $\lambda^n=1$. The action on one-dimensional subspaces factors through the projective quotient. Transvections generate the special linear group, and outside two small exceptions they are commutators.
proof: The determinant gives the first division by $q-1$; the scalar center gives the second. For simplicity, use the faithful primitive action on projective points, the abelian group of transvections with a fixed image line, normal in its stabilizer, and generation by its conjugates. A nontrivial normal subgroup must be transitive; the quotient becomes abelian, whereas the special linear group is perfect outside the exceptions. Hence the quotient is trivial.
pitfall: Simplicity is a statement about the projective quotient. The special linear group can have a nontrivial scalar center. At the exceptions, $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb F_2)\cong S_3$ and $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb F_3)\cong A_4$.
prompt: Follow the two quotients: determinant first, scalar center second.

worked.title: A simple group of order sixty
steps: The special linear subgroup has order $480/4=120$. Its center is $\{I,-I\}$.
The projective quotient has order $60$ and is simple. It is isomorphic to $A_5$.

reading.title: Determinants, scalar centers and simplicity
paragraphs: The determinant is onto $F^\times$ with kernel $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$. Over $\mathbb F_q$, divide the general linear group order by $q-1$. Commuting with every elementary matrix forces a central matrix to be scalar. In the special linear group its scalar satisfies $\lambda^n=1$.

Transvections generate the special linear group. Outside $n=2$ over the fields of orders two and three, they are commutators, so this group is perfect. Its action on projective points is doubly transitive; the kernel is its scalar center. Combining primitivity and conjugate root subgroups proves simplicity of $\operatorname{PSL}_n(F)$ with precisely those two exceptions.

For $n=2$, the order is $q(q^2-1)/\gcd(2,q-1)$. Thus the two exceptional projective groups are $S_3$ and $A_4$, whereas $\operatorname{PSL}_2(4)$ and $\operatorname{PSL}_2(5)$ are both isomorphic to $A_5$.

title: Blocks detect hidden quotients of an action

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: An action can look transitive on points yet move larger packets intact. A block is one such packet.
definition: \Delta\subseteq X\text{ a block}\iff\Delta\ne\varnothing,\quad g\Delta=\Delta\text{ or }g\Delta\cap\Delta=\varnothing\quad(\forall g\in G).
explanation: Assume $X$ is a transitive $G$-set and fix $x\in X$. Blocks containing $x$ correspond to subgroups between $G_x$ and $G$: a subgroup $H$ gives $Hx$. The trivial blocks are singletons and $X$. An action is primitive when no other blocks exist. Double transitivity means transitivity on ordered pairs of distinct points.
theorem: X\text{ primitive}\iff G_x\text{ maximal in }G;\qquad\text{doubly transitive}\Rightarrow\text{primitive}.
proof: The setwise stabilizer of a block containing $x$ contains $G_x$ and acts transitively on that block. Conversely $Hx$ is a block whenever $G_x\le H$. These constructions are inverse. If an action is doubly transitive, a non-singleton block can be moved while fixing one of its points; disjointness then forces it to contain every point.
pitfall: Primitive does not mean regular or faithful. A prime-degree transitive action is primitive, but need not be doubly transitive.
prompt: Compare the square action with the triangle action. Opposite pairs form blocks for the square.

worked.title: Opposite vertices of a square
steps: For $D_4$ acting on four vertices, $\Delta=\{0,2\}$ is a block.
Every symmetry either preserves $\Delta$ or sends it to $\{1,3\}$.
The action is transitive but imprimitive. The intermediate subgroup has order $4$, between a vertex stabilizer of order $2$ and $D_4$ of order $8$.

reading.title: Blocks, maximal stabilizers and double cosets
paragraphs: For a transitive action, a block containing $x$ is $Hx$ for a unique intermediate subgroup $G_x\le H\le G$. Thus primitivity is equivalent to maximality of the stabilizer. Double transitivity implies primitivity, since a block containing two points must contain every point.

Counting the fibers of $(h,k)\mapsto hxk$ gives $|HxK|=|H||K|/|H\cap xKx^{-1}|$. Under conjugation, element and subgroup stabilizers are respectively centralizers and normalizers. Hence $|g^G|=[G:C_G(g)]$ and the number of conjugates of $H$ is $[G:N_G(H)]$.

title: Coprime normal structure splits

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A normal subgroup can obstruct splitting. Coprime size and index remove that obstruction.
definition: N\trianglelefteq G,\quad \gcd(|N|,[G:N])=1;\qquad H\text{ complements }N\iff G=NH,\ N\cap H=1.
explanation: For a finite group, a Hall subgroup has order coprime to its index. Schur–Zassenhaus says that a normal Hall subgroup has a complement, so the group is a semidirect product. Existence of a complement and conjugacy of complements are separate assertions; the latter has an elementary treatment when the normal subgroup or quotient is solvable.
theorem: N\trianglelefteq G\text{ a Hall subgroup}\Longrightarrow G\cong N\rtimes H\text{ for some }|H|=[G:N].
proof: Induct on $|G|$. The Frattini argument reduces to a smaller normalizer unless a chosen Sylow subgroup of $N$ is normal in $G$. Continue reducing to an abelian normal subgroup. Its extension defect is a $2$-cocycle; averaging over the quotient annihilates the defect because the quotient order is invertible on the abelian Hall subgroup. A corrected section is a homomorphism and yields the complement.
pitfall: Normality is essential to this splitting statement. A semidirect product need not be direct, and without coprimality a complement can fail to exist.
prompt: Compare the normal subgroup of order three in the triangle group with the subgroup of order two in the cyclic group of order four.

worked.title: Split and non-split extensions
steps: $S_3=C_3\rtimes C_2$: a transposition supplies a complement to the normal subgroup $A_3$.
In $C_4$, the subgroup $C_2$ is normal but its order and index are not coprime.
The unique subgroup of order $2$ is the kernel itself, so it cannot be a complement. The extension of $C_2$ by $C_2$ does not split.

reading.title: Why a coprime normal subgroup splits
paragraphs: A Hall subgroup has order coprime to its index. Schur–Zassenhaus gives a complement to every normal Hall subgroup of a finite group. Thus $G=NH$, $N\cap H=1$ and $G\cong N\rtimes H$. Conjugacy of complements is obtained under the source’s solvability hypothesis on one of the two factors.

The coprimality is essential: the subgroup of order two in $C_4$ has no complement. For an abelian normal subgroup, averaging with the inverse of the coprime index removes the factor-set obstruction; induction reduces the general existence argument to this mechanism.

title: A section remembers the failure to split

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Maps & quotients
intuition: Choose one representative in each quotient class. Their products need not equal the representative of the product; the discrepancy is useful data.
explanation: A section is initially only a set map. Conjugation by $t(a)$ gives $\varphi(a)\in\operatorname{Aut}(N)$. Associativity imposes compatibility between $\varphi$ and $f$. If $N=A$ is abelian, the action is a genuine homomorphism and the defect is an additive $2$-cocycle. Replacing the section changes the cocycle by a coboundary.
proof: Expand $t(a)t(b)t(c)$ in its two associations to derive the cocycle identity. Under $t^{\prime}(a)=c(a)t(a)$, calculate the new defect: $f^{\prime}(a,b)=f(a,b)+c(a)+a\cdot c(b)-c(ab)$. Thus a class is zero exactly when a representative section can be corrected to a homomorphism. For nonabelian kernels, retain the full factor pair; the induced map to $\operatorname{Out}(N)$ is independent of the section.
pitfall: Equivalent extensions must respect the specified kernel and quotient maps. Isomorphic middle groups can define inequivalent extensions. A factor pair need not give an action into $\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ without an inner-automorphism correction.
prompt: Use carries in addition modulo four as the defect for a section of its quotient modulo two.

worked.title: A carry is a cocycle
steps: Write elements of $C_4$ as $2u+a$, where $u,a\in\{0,1\}$.
Addition is $(u,a)+(v,b)=(u+v+\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor,\ a+b\bmod2)$, with the first coordinate also modulo $2$.
The carry $f(1,1)=1$ obstructs a homomorphic section. Deleting the carry gives $C_2\times C_2$, a different extension.

reading.title: Factor sets, cohomology and changing a section
paragraphs: Fix an action of $H$ on an abelian group $A$, written additively. A normalized section of an extension gives multiplication $(a,x)(b,y)=(a+x\cdot b+f(x,y),xy)$. Associativity is exactly $x\cdot f(y,z)-f(xy,z)+f(x,yz)-f(x,y)=0$.

Changing the section by $t:H\to A$ replaces $f$ by $f+\delta t$, where $\delta t(x,y)=t(x)+x\cdot t(y)-t(xy)$. Thus $H^2(H,A)$ classifies extensions with fixed action and fixed identifications of kernel and quotient. The zero class is the split extension.

Within a split extension, complements correspond to crossed homomorphisms $d(xy)=d(x)+x\cdot d(y)$. Conjugating by $A$ changes a crossed homomorphism by a principal one, giving the $H^1$ description. These equivalence relations are part of the classification, not optional notation.
