title: Peel away commutators

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: One commutator subgroup removes the abelian information. Solvability means that repeating this process eventually leaves nothing.
definition: G^{(0)}=G,\qquad G^{(i+1)}=[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}],\qquad G\text{ solvable}\iff G^{(r)}=1\text{ for some }r.
explanation: Solvability is equivalent to admitting a finite subnormal series with abelian factors. It passes to subgroups and quotients, and if both a normal subgroup and its quotient are solvable, so is the whole group. For finite groups it is equivalent to having only prime-order composition factors, or elementary abelian chief factors.
theorem: G\text{ finite solvable},\ |G|=mn,\ (m,n)=1\Longrightarrow\text{Hall subgroups of order }m\text{ exist, are conjugate, and contain every }m\text{-subgroup}.
proof: For the derived-series criterion, each abelian factor forces the next commutator subgroup into the next term. Closure under extensions follows by first descending into the solvable kernel and then through its derived series. For Hall existence and conjugacy, induct using a minimal normal subgroup: in a solvable group it is elementary abelian. Pass to the quotient, then lift and use coprime splitting or the corresponding elementary induction.
pitfall: Solvable is weaker than nilpotent. The factors in a solvable series are abelian; the whole group need not be. Hall existence for every coprime divisor characterises finite solvable groups, but one Hall subgroup alone does not.
prompt: Follow the derived series of the symmetric group on four points; compare with the group on three points.

worked.title: Three steps for the symmetric group
steps: $[S_4,S_4]=A_4$: the sign map gives an abelian quotient, and commutators generate the three-cycles.
The three abelian successive quotients show that $S_4$ has derived length $3$. It is not nilpotent because its Sylow subgroups are not all normal.

reading.title: Equivalent series, Hall subgroups and affine actions
paragraphs: Solvability is equivalent to a normal or subnormal series with abelian factors. It passes to subgroups and quotients and is closed under extensions and finite direct products. For a group with a composition series, it means every composition factor has prime order; equivalently its chief factors are elementary abelian.

A finite solvable group has Hall subgroups for every selection of primes. Such Hall subgroups are conjugate, and every subgroup using only those primes lies in one. Conversely existence of Hall subgroups for all prime selections characterizes finite solvability.

A faithful finite solvable primitive permutation group has a regular elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup. Identify the points with that vector space: translations give the normal subgroup and the point stabilizer acts linearly. This places the group inside an affine general linear group.

Burnside’s two-prime theorem is proved using characters later. The odd-order theorem says every finite group of odd order is solvable; its proof lies far beyond these notes. A further criterion detects nonsolvability through nonidentity elements of pairwise coprime orders satisfying $xy=z$; it is a structural theorem, not an efficient search algorithm.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

title: Central layers control the whole group

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A central series lets you remove one layer at a time, with each layer commuting with everything that remains.
explanation: A group is nilpotent exactly when its lower central series reaches $1$, or its upper central series reaches $G$, in finitely many steps. For finite groups this is also equivalent to every Sylow subgroup being normal, to being the direct product of the Sylow subgroups, and to every proper subgroup being properly contained in its normalizer.
theorem: G\text{ finite nilpotent}\iff G\cong\prod_{p\mid |G|}P_p;\qquad P/\Phi(P)\cong\mathbb F_p^d\quad(P\text{ a finite }p\text{-group}).
proof: A nontrivial finite $p$-group has nontrivial center by the class equation. Apply the argument repeatedly to central quotients. For a finite nilpotent group, the normalizer condition forces Sylow normalizers to be the whole group. Conversely normal Sylow subgroups of coprime orders commute and form a direct product. For the Frattini quotient, maximal subgroups of a $p$-group have index $p$, so all commutators and $p$th powers lie in their intersection.
pitfall: Derived and central series are different. Every nilpotent group is solvable, but $S_3$ is solvable and not nilpotent. Finite nilpotent groups need not be abelian.
prompt: For the quaternion group, identify its center and its quotient. Compare with the dihedral group of order eight.

worked.title: A nonabelian group of class two
steps: In $Q_8$, commutators lie in $\{\pm1\}$, which is central.
Thus $\gamma_2(Q_8)=\{\pm1\}$ and $\gamma_3(Q_8)=1$.
The upper series is $1<\{\pm1\}<Q_8$. Both central series have length $2$.

reading.title: Central series and the finite nilpotence tests
paragraphs: The lower central series is $\gamma_1(G)=G$, $\gamma_{i+1}(G)=[\gamma_i(G),G]$. The upper central series starts at $1$ and pulls back the centers of successive quotients. Termination of the first at $1$ is equivalent to the second reaching $G$. Nilpotent groups are solvable.

For a finite group, nilpotence is equivalent to all Sylow subgroups being normal, to their internal direct product, to all maximal subgroups being normal, and to every proper subgroup being properly contained in its normalizer. Finiteness matters: these are not unrestricted equivalences.

The product of finite normal nilpotent subgroups is nilpotent; their product is the Fitting subgroup. In a finite solvable group it is an important source of normal structure. In $S_3$ the Fitting subgroup is $C_3$, while the whole group is solvable but not nilpotent.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

title: Bilinear rules become linear maps

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: A tensor product packages every bilinear calculation into one linear object. Pure tensors are building blocks, not every possible tensor.
explanation: For a right $R$-module $U$ and a left $R$-module $V$, the tensor product is generated by symbols $u\otimes v$ subject to additivity and the balancing relation. Over a field, bases give a product basis. For finite-dimensional $U$, a dual vector and a vector define the rank-one map $u\mapsto\varphi(u)v$.
proof: Choose a basis $e_i$ of $U$ with dual basis $e_i^*$. The tensors $e_i^*\otimes f_j$ map to the matrix units, so the displayed map is bijective. Its formula is independent of the chosen bases. For group modules, use $g\varphi=\varphi\circ g^{-1}$ and $g(\varphi\otimes v)=g\varphi\otimes gv$; evaluation then proves equivariance.
pitfall: The balancing relation requires the correct left/right module sides. A general tensor is a sum of pure tensors; for example a rank-two matrix is not one outer product.
prompt: Build two rank-one operators and add them. A basis matrix isolates exactly one input and one output coordinate.

worked.title: Two rank-one pieces make the identity
steps: For $U=F^2$, let $e_1,e_2$ be the standard basis and $e_1^*,e_2^*$ its dual.
The tensor $e_1^*\otimes e_1$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(x,0)$; $e_2^*\otimes e_2$ sends it to $(0,y)$.
Their sum represents the identity. Its matrix has rank $2$, so it cannot be represented by a single pure tensor.

reading.title: Balancing, direct sums and equivariance
paragraphs: The maps $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$ and $m\mapsto1\otimes m$ show $R\otimes_R M\cong M$. Tensor products distribute over direct sums because the same balanced bilinear map can be specified separately on each summand.

For finite-dimensional $U$, $U^*\otimes_F V\cong\operatorname{Hom}_F(U,V)$ via $\varphi\otimes v\mapsto[u\mapsto\varphi(u)v]$. For group representations, use the contragredient action on the dual and conjugation on Hom; the map is then equivariant.

A linear group action extends uniquely by linearity to a group-algebra module. If the group is finite, finite generation over the group algebra is equivalent to finite vector-space dimension, since the algebra itself has a finite basis indexed by group elements.

title: An algebra splits into matrix blocks

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: A semisimple algebra looks complicated until its simple modules reveal independent matrix blocks.
definition: M\text{ semisimple}\iff M=\bigoplus_i S_i\text{ with each }S_i\text{ simple}.
explanation: Here all algebras are finite-dimensional over a field and have an identity, and modules are finite-dimensional and unital. A module is semisimple exactly when each submodule has a complement. An algebra is semisimple exactly when its regular left module is semisimple. Matrix blocks classify the resulting algebra, while multiplicities classify its modules.
theorem: A\text{ semisimple}\iff A\cong\prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i),\qquad D_i\text{ finite-dimensional division algebras}.
proof: Decompose the regular module into isotypic pieces $n_iS_i$. Schur gives zero homomorphisms between nonisomorphic simple modules and division rings of endomorphisms on each simple. Thus its endomorphism ring is a product of matrix rings. Right multiplication identifies $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $\operatorname{End}_A(A)$; taking opposite rings recovers the claimed decomposition. Over an algebraically closed field, the division algebras are the field itself.
pitfall: Semisimple does not mean commutative. A simple algebra may have many proper left ideals: simplicity excludes proper nonzero two-sided ideals. The finite-dimensional hypothesis matters.
prompt: Follow each relationship from the regular module to its endomorphisms. Then count the dimensions of the matrix blocks in the worked example.

worked.title: The group algebra of the triangle group
steps: Over $\mathbb C$, $S_3$ has irreducible degrees $1,1,2$.
Hence $\mathbb C S_3\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C\times M_2(\mathbb C)$ and its dimension is $1^2+1^2+2^2=6$.
There are $2^3=8$ two-sided ideals, one for each choice of whole blocks. The regular module contains the two-dimensional simple twice.

reading.title: From complements to matrix blocks
paragraphs: Throughout this discussion algebras and modules are finite-dimensional over a field. A module is semisimple exactly when every submodule is a direct summand. Submodules and quotients remain semisimple. A unital algebra is semisimple exactly when its regular module is semisimple.

Choose representatives $S_i$ of the simple modules. Schur’s lemma makes $\operatorname{End}_A(S_i)$ a division algebra and kills Hom between different representatives. On $\bigoplus_i n_iS_i$, endomorphisms consequently form a product of matrix algebras. Right multiplication gives $\operatorname{End}_A(A)\cong A^{\mathrm{op}}$, which accounts for the opposite-ring convention in the proof.

The natural column module is the only simple module of $M_n(D)$ up to isomorphism, and its regular module consists of $n$ copies. Matrix units show every nonzero two-sided ideal is the whole matrix algebra. Ideals in a product split by factors, so a semisimple algebra has exactly the ideals obtained by selecting whole simple blocks.

Over an algebraically closed field, a finite-dimensional division algebra is the field itself: every element has an eigenvalue, and its difference from that scalar cannot be invertible. Thus the blocks are ordinary matrix algebras over the ground field.

title: The radical is what simple modules cannot see

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: The radical collects the obstruction to semisimplicity. Removing it leaves exactly the matrix blocks seen by simple modules.
explanation: For a finite-dimensional unital algebra, the Jacobson radical is nilpotent, is the largest nilpotent two-sided ideal, and is the smallest left submodule of the regular module with semisimple quotient. The quotient $A/J(A)$ is semisimple and has the same simple modules as $A$. These descriptions fit the commutative radical picture into noncommutative representation theory.
proof: A nilpotent ideal annihilates every simple module: otherwise its image is the whole module, and iteration contradicts nilpotence. Intersecting annihilators therefore contains all nilpotent ideals. Finite length and the semisimple quotient show this intersection is itself nilpotent. For a module, pass to the quotient by $J(A)M$ and use the semisimplicity of $A/J(A)$; the socle is the part already annihilated by the radical.
pitfall: The radical is nilpotent here because the algebra is finite-dimensional. For a general commutative ring the nilradical need not be nilpotent. Nilpotent elements need not individually form an ideal in a noncommutative algebra.
prompt: Use the upper triangular algebra: erase strictly upper triangular entries and watch the diagonal factors survive.

worked.title: Upper triangular matrices
steps: For $T_2(F)$, the strictly upper triangular matrices form an ideal $J$ with $J^2=0$.
The diagonal map has kernel $J$ and image $F\times F$. Thus $T_2(F)/J\cong F\times F$.
On the natural column module, the socle is the first coordinate line; the quotient is the other one-dimensional simple. The module is not the direct sum of those lines as a $T_2(F)$-module.

reading.title: The radical, unitisation and common fixed vectors
paragraphs: In finite dimension, sums of nilpotent two-sided ideals are nilpotent: sufficiently long products must contain enough factors from one ideal. This gives a largest nilpotent ideal. Intersections of submodules with semisimple quotients again have semisimple quotient, yielding a smallest such submodule.

For a unital algebra these constructions equal the common annihilator of simple modules, namely $J(A)$. Hence $A/J(A)$ is semisimple and $A$ is semisimple exactly when it has no nonzero nilpotent ideals.

An algebra without identity embeds as an ideal in $F\oplus A$, with multiplication $(r,a)(s,b)=(rs,rb+sa+ab)$. A nonzero finite-dimensional algebra without nonzero nilpotent ideals acquires its own identity through its semisimple block decomposition.

The source’s nilpotent-span theorem and its application to the algebra generated by differences $h-I$ provide a common fixed nonzero vector for a unipotent matrix group. Inducting on the quotient then yields simultaneous upper unitriangular form. “Every generator is nilpotent” by itself is insufficient: the associative algebra they generate need not be nilpotent.

reading.title: Module layers and matrix-ring modules
paragraphs: For a finite-dimensional unital algebra, $\operatorname{rad}M=J(A)M$ and $\operatorname{soc}M=\{m:J(A)m=0\}$. Iterating gives radical and socle filtrations. The successive layers are semisimple, but the full module may glue them in a nontrivial way.

Matrix units identify modules over $M_n(A)$ with modules over $A$: take $e_{11}M$ in one direction and column vectors in the other. This explains why matrix rings share simple-module structure with the coefficient algebra even though their vector-space dimensions differ. Free and projective modules should not be confused with simple modules.

title: Character values are algebraic integers

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: Traces are sums of roots of unity. That arithmetic information forces divisibility that linear algebra alone does not reveal.
definition: \alpha\text{ algebraic integer}\iff f(\alpha)=0\text{ for some monic }f\in\mathbb Z[X].
explanation: Algebraic integers form a ring, and a rational algebraic integer is an ordinary integer. Since a finite-order complex matrix has roots of unity as eigenvalues, every character value is an algebraic integer. For an irreducible character, the scalar by which a conjugacy-class sum acts is also an algebraic integer.
theorem: \frac{|g^G|\chi(g)}{\chi(1)}\text{ is an algebraic integer};\qquad\chi(1)\mid|G|\quad(\chi\text{ irreducible over }\mathbb C).
proof: Class sums multiply with integer structure constants in the center of $\mathbb CG$. Their scalar actions satisfy monic integer polynomials, by the characteristic polynomial of this multiplication. Row orthogonality expresses $|G|/\chi(1)$ as a sum of products of these algebraic integers with conjugate character values. It is rational, so it is an integer.
pitfall: Character values need not be rational or integral as ordinary numbers. Divisibility concerns the degree of a complex irreducible character, not an arbitrary representation dimension.
prompt: Compare degrees with the group order, then compare ordinary integer character values with the golden-ratio values in the alternating group of degree five.

worked.title: The degree test
steps: The irreducible degrees of $A_5$ are $1,3,3,4,5$. Each divides $60$.
The three-dimensional characters take $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and $(1-\sqrt5)/2$ on the five-cycle classes.
These values are not integers, but both satisfy the monic polynomial $X^2-X-1$.

reading.title: The arithmetic behind character divisibility
paragraphs: A rational root of a monic integer polynomial has denominator one. Algebraic integers form a ring: finitely many generators lie in a finitely generated integer module stable under multiplication, and the determinant argument gives a monic equation for any sum or product.

Character values are sums of roots of unity. Class sums multiply with integer coefficients; their scalar actions on irreducibles therefore satisfy monic integer equations. Row orthogonality then expresses $|G|/\chi(1)$ as an algebraic integer. Since it is rational, it is an integer.

If a normalized nonzero character value is an algebraic integer, all its Galois conjugates have absolute value at most one. Its nonzero integer norm forces equality everywhere. This is the arithmetic step that turns a nonzero normalized trace into a scalar action.

title: A small conjugacy class forces normal structure

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A group whose order uses only two primes cannot hide a nonabelian simple factor. Character arithmetic explains why.
explanation: Burnside proves that every finite group of order $p^aq^b$ is solvable. The key character-theoretic obstruction says that a nonabelian finite simple group has no conjugacy class of size a nontrivial prime power. Prime-power here describes the size of the class, not the order of its representative.
proof: For the class-size obstruction, combine orthogonality with integrality of central character scalars to force a nontrivial irreducible representation to have a nontrivial scalar kernel, contradicting simplicity. To deduce solvability, suppose a nonabelian simple counterexample has order $p^aq^b$. A nonidentity central element of a Sylow $q$-subgroup has centralizer containing that Sylow subgroup; its class size is a power of $p$. The obstruction rules this out. Induction on normal subgroups then gives solvability.
pitfall: Do not confuse this theorem with the orbit-counting lemma also named after Burnside. A group of prime-power order has nontrivial center; the class-size argument addresses the two-prime case.
prompt: Follow the centralizer index: a central element of a Sylow subgroup leaves only the other prime in its conjugacy-class size.

worked.title: Why order thirty-six is solvable
steps: $36=2^2\cdot3^2$. Every simple composition factor has order involving at most the primes $2$ and $3$.
The class-size obstruction excludes any nonabelian simple factor of that order type.
Every simple factor therefore has prime order. This is the composition-factor criterion for solvability.

reading.title: Prime-power class sizes and counting commutators
paragraphs: For a conjugacy class of nontrivial prime-power size, combine a Bézout relation for an irreducible degree coprime to that prime with integrality of the central scalar. The normalized nonzero character value must have absolute value one, so the element acts as a scalar. Orthogonality ensures a suitable nontrivial irreducible exists; simplicity then fails.

If a nonabelian simple group had order $p^aq^b$, take a nonidentity central element of a Sylow $q$-subgroup. Its centralizer contains that Sylow subgroup, making its conjugacy class a nontrivial power of $p$. The obstruction rules this out, and induction over normal subgroups proves solvability.

Character methods also count solutions of commutator equations. For the convention $[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$, the number of pairs with $[x,y]=g$ is $|G|\sum_{\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}(G)}\chi(g)/\chi(1)$. At the identity this becomes $|G|$ times the number of conjugacy classes, agreeing with direct counting of commuting pairs.

title: Fixed-point-free motions form a subgroup

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: If no nonidentity motion fixes two points, the motions fixing no point assemble into a normal subgroup after adding the identity.
explanation: For a finite faithful permutation group satisfying this condition, the identity together with the fixed-point-free elements is the Frobenius kernel. It is a regular normal subgroup. A point stabilizer is a complement, so the group is a semidirect product. The closure assertion is the surprising part: it does not follow just by inspecting fixed points of a product.
proof: Let the point stabilizer be $H$. Distinct conjugates intersect trivially, so induction of nontrivial characters of $H$ has tightly controlled inner products. Frobenius reciprocity constructs a character whose kernel is exactly the claimed set. This proves closure and normality; the count then shows $|N|=|X|$, giving regularity and the complement.
pitfall: The fixed-point condition must hold for every nonidentity group element. A merely transitive action need not have such a kernel. The word “Frobenius” here names a permutation-group theorem, distinct from reciprocity.
prompt: Consider affine transformations of a finite prime field. Nonidentity translations fix no point; a nontranslation fixes exactly one.

worked.title: Affine motions of five points
steps: Let $G=\{x\mapsto ax+b:a\in\mathbb F_5^\times,b\in\mathbb F_5\}$, of order $20$.
For $a=1,b\ne0$, there is no fixed point. For $a\ne1$, the unique fixed point is $x=b/(1-a)$.
The translations form the normal kernel $C_5$, and maps fixing zero form a complement $C_4$.

reading.title: The Frobenius kernel and its character-theoretic proof
paragraphs: In a finite faithful transitive action with more than one point, assume no nonidentity element fixes two points. Point stabilizers intersect trivially. Counting their conjugates shows that the identity together with the fixed-point-free elements has exactly as many elements as the set being acted on.

Counting does not show closure. Frobenius’s theorem supplies that missing step using induced characters and orthogonality: the set is a normal subgroup, acting regularly. A point stabilizer is a complement. In the affine action of $\mathbb F_q\rtimes\mathbb F_q^\times$, the kernel consists of translations.

title: Fibers of a linear map become a vector space

source.title: MH3220 Algebra II — Kay Jin Lim, 25 July 2026

subject: Maps & quotients
intuition: Every fiber is a translated copy of the kernel. Replace that entire copy by one point and the map becomes a bijection onto its image.
explanation: Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map over a field. The quotient has vector addition and scalar multiplication inherited from $V$. If two representatives differ by a kernel vector, their images agree, so the displayed map is well-defined. Every image vector has a representative, and only the zero coset maps to zero.
proof: Prove well-definedness using $T(v-u)=0$. Linearity is inherited directly from $T$. Surjectivity follows from the definition of the image, and injectivity from equality of fibers. In finite dimensions, extend a basis of the kernel to a basis of $V$; the images of the new basis vectors form a basis of the image.
pitfall: The image can be a proper subspace of the stated codomain. Quotienting by the kernel gives the image, not automatically the whole codomain.
prompt: Choose the zero matrix, a rank-one matrix, and an invertible matrix over the finite field. Compare the sizes of their fibers.

worked.title: A projection over the field with three elements
steps: Let $T(x,y)=(x,0)$ over $\mathbb F_3$. The kernel contains $(0,0),(0,1),(0,2)$.
There are three fibers, indexed by $x$, each containing three vectors.
Thus the nine-element domain becomes a three-element quotient, isomorphic to the image line.

title: One relation changes the arithmetic

source.title: MH3220 Algebra II — Kay Jin Lim, 25 July 2026

subject: Fields & polynomials
intuition: Adjoining a symbol becomes concrete when one polynomial relation tells you how to reduce every higher power.
explanation: Every residue class has a unique representative $u+v\alpha$, because the modulus is monic of degree two. The quotient therefore has $p^2$ elements. Addition works coefficient by coefficient. Multiplication expands first, then uses the defining relation. The same construction gives fields, products of fields, or rings with nilpotents depending on factorisation.
theorem: A\text{ a field}\iff X^2+bX+c\text{ irreducible over }\mathbb F_p.
proof: Polynomial division gives unique representatives. If the modulus is irreducible, every nonzero lower-degree polynomial is coprime to it; Bézout gives a multiplicative inverse in the quotient. If the modulus factors, its proper factors give nonzero classes whose product is zero. Repeated roots yield nilpotents; distinct roots yield a product by the Chinese remainder theorem.
pitfall: No roots implies irreducibility for degrees two and three. The same root test is insufficient in degree four or higher.
prompt: Over the field with three elements, compare a repeated-root modulus, a split modulus, and an irreducible quadratic.

worked.title: Three different rings of size nine
steps: $\mathbb F_3[X]/(X^2)$ has a nonzero nilpotent $\alpha$ with $\alpha^2=0$.
$X^2-1=(X-1)(X+1)$ gives $\mathbb F_3[X]/(X^2-1)\cong\mathbb F_3\times\mathbb F_3$.
$X^2+1$ has no root in $\mathbb F_3$, so its quotient is the field with nine elements.
